newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Britain boosts EU anti-smoking campaign.
newsitem.headline: Britain boosts EU anti-smoking campaign.

text.p: European efforts to combat smoking were boosted on Thursday by the new British Labour government's pledge to take action but agreement on a package of measures is still a long way off, EU officials said.
Campaigners say that 500 people a day die of tobacco-related diseases in Europe but the number of smokers remains steady as children and teenagers take up the habit.

"...We are committed to banning tobacco advertising as an essential first step in building an effective strategy to deal with smoking," British Public Health Minister Tessa Jowell told a meeting of EU health ministers.

Jowell said Britain would hold a summit of national and international experts in July to examine options for reducing tobacco consumption and lay the basis for an overall strategy paper later this year.
Britain broadly agreed with European Commission proposals to reduce tobacco consumption, she said.
"But there are unresolved legal question about its scope, as well as practical issues, such as the impact on sports," Jowell said, referring to sports sponsorship by tobacco companies.
"The U.K. government is working up plans to remove advertising and promotion of tobacco in a way that does not damage those sports," she said.
EU Health Commissioner Padraig Flynn welcomed Britain's change of attitude which he hoped would soon lead to agreement on an EU ban on tobacco advertising and sponsorship.
But European tobacco producers were sceptical.

"Even with a change in the position of the UK government there would still not be enough support in the Council to adopt this proposal," Robert Toet, Chairman of the Confederation of European Community Cigarette Manufacturers, said in a statement.
Germany, the Netherlands, Greece and Denmark have been blocking an EU-wide ban while Austria, Italy and Denmark also have reservations about other proposed EU anti-tobacco measures.
The tobacco industry has voluntarily agreed with several member state governments not to advertise near schools or in teenager magazines, he added.
But the International Union Against Cancer, a coalition of charities, disagreed.

"Those who wish to maintain the industry, and who do so only through their success in addicting youngsters to nicotine, should consider the human, social and economic consequences of their actions," it said in a statement.
It added that although the tobacco industry generated large tax revenues, it also caused massive health costs and loss of earnings due to early retirement and sickness.
